# **Pull Requests**
***

## What is a pull request? 
***

Recall that in the initial description of branches, you learned that branches can be used for development of a new part of a project, separate from the stable version of a repository. A {{< glossary "pull request" >}} is a way to take a collection of commits on a branch and request to {{< glossary "merge">}} those into another {{< glossary "branch">}}, typically `main`. A pull request will provide a list of each file that is changed in the branch, as well as the difference between each file and the version of that file on the branch that you are trying to merge your changes into. While you can review your own pull requests, GitHub also has features that make it convenient for collaborators to review your pull requests. 

## How to make a pull request 
***

In the previous section, you worked locally to make the visualizations that Collab O. Rator had asked you for, and you staged, committed, and pushed these changes. Recall that you were working on a branch called `study_comparison`. Let's take a look at this branch on GitHub. 

- [ ] Navigate back to "https://github.com/your_username/infant_gut_analysis" (replacing your username). 
- [ ] Click underneath the repository name where is says "Branches". This should take you to a page that shows you the existing branches (this should include `main` and `study_comparison`). 
- [ ] Click on `study_comparison`. 
- [ ] You should see a yellow banner with a green button that says "Compare & pull request". Click on this button. 

This set of steps will bring you to a page where you can make your pull request. The first thing to note is the panel at the top of the page, which gives you the base branch (this will by default be `main`) and the compare branch (this will be the branch you've been working on, in this case `study_comparison`). There is an arrow, showing that you are trying to merge the updates that you've made in the compare branch into the base branch. 

```{r, fig.alt="Example open pull request page", echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center"}
ottrpal::include_slide("https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1TEi1D35oiiC21mYR0cKjWuOOpuxm3fTGyCXSqFmjL3I/edit?slide=id.h57fc035897434697_0_0&pli=1#slide=id.h57fc035897434697_0_0")
```

There are a few useful components of this page in which you make a pull request:

- You have a spot to add a title and a description. 
- If you scroll down, you'll see a list of commits that make up this pull request along with the commit messages, and a view of each of the files changed with details of what was changed. 
- On the right panel next to the title you'll see an option for reviewers. If other users have access to this repository, then you can add them as a reviewer. Depending on how they have configured their notification preferences, they may get an email notification that you've requested a review from them. It is good practice for you to also reach out to them and send them the link to your pull request to review! 

:::{.reproducibility_box}
::::{.reproducibility_box_header}
Reproducibility considerations
::::
::::{.inner_block}
Components of a good pull requests include:

- A concise but descriptive title.
- A description of the changes you want to merge. This is a good place to list files added and modified and give a quick description of those changes. Give plenty of context; you've likely been thinking about the code you want to merge more recently than your collaborator who will review it. 
  - One good way to describe changes is in a checklist of what you've done.
  - It can also be helpful to include a checklist of what is left to do, especially if your pull request is a work in progress.
- A request for code review (make specific requests: do you want your collaborator to review all changes? do you want them to focus on a specific file or part of an analysis? do you just a bigger picture review to see if your approach to the problem makes sense?).

For additional suggestions on making good pull requests, you can read more in [this reproducibility course](https://jhudatascience.org/Adv_Reproducibility_in_Cancer_Informatics/engaging-in-code-review---as-an-author.html). Also see [this real-world example of a pull request](https://github.com/AlexsLemonade/OpenPBTA-analysis/pull/741) with these components, followed by back-and-forth between the author and reviewer to iterate on the proposed changes to the analysis. 
::::
:::

Navigate to your pull request page and do the following:

- [ ] Add a title for your pull request.
- [ ] Add a description. 
- [ ] Click "Create pull request" button.

## Merging or closing pull requests 
***

Once you have created a pull request, it is referred to as "open", and the two potential actions are to merge it or close it. 

### Merging pull requests 

Imagine that you submitted a pull request, you or your collaborator has decided that the changes look good, and you want to integrate the changes from your development branch into the base branch. This is called merging your pull request. In most cases, you will see a box that says "No conflicts with base branch", and you can click the button that says "Merge pull request". However, in some cases, you will not be able to merge until you resolve merge conflicts. See the [troubleshooting section](https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bio-version-control/#troubleshooting-git-and-github) for more information about merge conflicts and how to resolve them. 

### Closing pull requests

If you close a pull request without merging it, this means that you've decided not to integrate the changes from the compare branch into the base branch. This may happen if you decide to go in another direction with an analysis. You can close a pull request by clicking the "Close pull request" button at the bottom of the pull request page. It is important to close pull requests that are no longer active so that the set of open pull requests accurately represents the current state of the project. 

```{r, fig.alt="Pull request page", echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center"}
ottrpal::include_slide("hhttps://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1QjS4NwVgB_oZX5YCHKCzVe9x4XRWhNv-N7iP26JXHXo/edit?slide=id.h175e18de373b618c_0_0#slide=id.h175e18de373b618c_0_0")
```

The image above shows what the pull requests page might look like for this repository, if there were another open pull request for a different component of the project, and if there were previously merged or closed pull requests. Like the issues page, the pull requests page for a repository provides a searchable history of works in progress (open pull requests), and completed tasks (closed pull requests). This can be helpful to you, a collaborator, or someone interested in the process of your scientific project, to understand the major contributions to the repository. 

## Additional notes on pull requests 
***

While your pull request is open, any additional changes that you commit and push to this branch will be automatically added to the pull request. 

A pull request should be a set of changes that address a certain component of an analysis. Try to avoid combining multiple parts of a project in a single pull request. If you decide to start working on a different part of a project, you can create a new branch for this, and eventually submit a new pull request from that branch. 

Separating different parts of a project into multiple branches and pull requests is a good way to stay organized for complex projects that have multiple components in development at the same time. Using multiple branches and focused pull requests, each including a set of related commits, can make it easier to review the pull requests and to identify when and why changes were introduced to a project. Changes to files that depend on each other but relate to different issues can be addressed in a series of "stacked" pull requests (check out [GitHub's documentation about stacked pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/stacked-pull-requests) for more information).
